topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Digit Emergence
target_audience: Undergraduate physics students or math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Hook: An Unexpected Connection
lecture_lines: Two blocks collide: small mass m, large mass M.
They bounce between a wall and each other.
For M=100m, we see exactly 31 collisions.
Surprisingly, this counts the digits of pi.
animations: Fade in text '#F8F9FA' labeled 'The Unexpected Connection'.
Animate a connection line '#E9ECEF' appearing between two dots.
Highlight the connection point with a '#FFC107' flash.
Fade out all elements to transition to next section.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
lecture_lines: Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and energy.
Energy is half mass times velocity squared.
animations: Fade in label '#F8F9FA' for 'Conservation of Energy'.
Visualize energy flow as a '#20C997' smooth curve.
Highlight conserved quantity value '#FD7E14' within the curve.

sections.title: The Phase Space Mapping
lecture_lines: Instead of time, map velocities (v1, v2).
Collisions jump the state along this path.
animations: Fade in grid lines '#495057' representing phase space.

Draw trajectory path '#6610F2' as the point evolves.
Highlight the final position with a '#D63384' circle.
Scale up the entire grid to emphasize the mapping.

sections.title: Geometric Unfolding
lecture_lines: Collisions map to reflections in a wedge.
The wedge angle depends on mass ratio.
animations: Animate the unfolding process using '#17A2B8' rotation.
Emphasize the final area using a '#FFC107' fill.

sections.title: Conclusion: Why Pi?
lecture_lines: Geometry maps reflection count to pi digits.
Higher mass ratios reveal more digits.
It's an elegant, hidden geometric law.
